Tricks from OpenAI gpt-oss YOU 🫵 can use with transformers

📅 11 Sep 2025 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2573 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • OpenAI recently released their GPT-OSS series of models.
  • In this blog post, we talk about all the upgrades in-depth, and how they become part of the transformers toolkit so other models (current and future) can benefit from them.
  • Best part: Most of these features should work across all major models within transformers!
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

OpenAI recently released their GPT-OSS series of models. The models feature some novel techniques like MXFP4 quantization, efficient kernels, a brand new chat format, and more. To enable the release of gpt-oss through transformers, we have upgraded the library considerably. The updates make it very efficient to load, run, and fine-tune the models.

In this blog post, we talk about all the upgrades in-depth, and how they become part of the transformers toolkit so other models (current and future) can benefit from them. Providing clean implementations of new methods in transformers also allows the community to promptly understand and adopt them. Frameworks such as MLX, llama.cpp or vLLM can use the transformers code as a reference to build their own implementations.

For this release, we worked on:.

Best part: Most of these features should work across all major models within transformers!

A kernel is a specialized, compact program that runs on accelerators to execute tasks like matrix multiplications, activations, or normalizations. In eager PyTorch, operations trigger individual kernels sequentially, which is straightforward but can incur extra memory transfers and launch overheads. PyTorch 2.0's torch.compile with backends like TorchInductor addresses this by automatically fusing and optimizing kernels, delivering 2–10× performance gains.

Recent findings suggest that in addition, the community has created custom kernels for frequent combinations of operations, not just individual PyTorch ops like matmul. For example, Flash Attention was created to optimize the critical attention block that defines the transformers architecture, and is present in many models including most LLMs. By carefully combining all the attention operations inside a single kernel, memory transfers are minimized, memory use is reduced, and speedups can be achieved.

In a recent development, the problem is that all these various kernels are available in separate libraries, which creates a dependency bloat if they were to be added to the transformers library. Furthermore, these kernels are not just Python code, they consist of low-level cuda code, glued together with C++ and exposed through a Python layer. This means they have to be compiled in the target system, which in turn requires whatever build system is required by each kernel library.

Recent findings suggest that the kernels package solves this problem by downloading pre-built binaries of supported kernels from the Hub. You just indicate the kernel you want to use, and kernels will look for a version compatible with your system and download it on first use.

GPT-OSS, a Mixture of Experts (MoE) model, is a massive user of Kernels from the Hub. It leverages several custom kernels:.

Let's take a look at the first two ones.

Recent findings suggest that behind the scenes, the decorators (1 and 2) simply point to community-contributed kernels. For example, RMSNorm comes from liger_kernels, while the MegaBlocksMoeMLP kernel comes from megablocks. Depending on your device (CUDA or ROCm) and whether you’re training or running inference, the right kernel is pulled in automatically.

This design is both specific and general: the RMSNorm liger kernels are already being reused across multiple models, and the MoE kernel could be applied to future MoEs as well.

Because kernels pulls code from the Hub, you have to opt-in to this feature by passing use_kernels=True in your model instantiation, as shown below. We enable INFO logging in the example so you can easily verify that downloadable kernels are in use.

These kernels are not compatible with mxfp4, so inference will happen in bfloat16 if you use them. Please, benchmark your system for the best combination in memory and throughput that suits your project!

Running a quick generation yields log messages like.

Figure 1 reveals that, in the system we tested, these kernels work best for larger batch sizes. We always recommend to benchmark any performance-related changes as closely to your production conditions as possible.

You can explore and play with the benchmarking script here.

In a recent development, openAI gpt-oss models use attention sinks, which improves quality and facilitates the use of longer contexts. The vLLM team added this feature to the latest version of Flash Attention (Flash Attention 3), and the resulting custom kernel is available on the Hub. Presently, this kernel is compatible with the Hopper architecture. If you have one, this is the way to enable it:.

Industry observers note that large language models are memory-hungry. Quantization reduces memory footprint by storing weights (and sometimes activations) in lower-precision formats. For reference, FP32 uses 32 bits per number and BF16 uses 16. By reducing bit width, we trade some precision for smaller models and faster memory movement.

If you want a visual primer on quantization trade-offs, Maarten Grootendorst’s article is excellent: A Visual Guide to Quantization.

Recent findings suggest that MXFP4 is a 4-bit floating format with E2M1 layout: 1 sign bit, 2 exponent bits, and 1 mantissa bit, as shown in Figure 2. On its own, E2M1 is very coarse. MXFP4 compensates with blockwise scaling:.

This blockwise scheme lets MXFP4 keep range while using very few bits. In practice, GPT-OSS 20B fits in roughly 16 GB of VRAM and GPT-OSS 120B fits in roughly 80 GB when MXFP4 is active, which is the difference between “cannot load” and “can run on a single GPU.” The catch is that matrix multiplies now have to respect block scales. Doing this efficiently at scale requires dedicated kernels.

Recent findings suggest that transformers now includes native support for MXFP4, leveraging optimized triton (MXFP4) kernels for enhanced performance. This builds on the community-driven kernel distribution discussed earlier, utilizing pre-compiled kernels from the Hub to simplify deployment.

To check if a model supports MXFP4, inspect its configuration:.

If 'quant_method': 'mxfp4' is present, the model will automatically use the MXFP4 pathway with Triton kernels when supported.

Thanks to this pull request, you can fine-tune gpt-oss models and save them directly to the Hub in MXFP4 format, streamlining deployment with optimized performance.

If these constraints are not met, transformers falls back to a higher-precision path (bfloat16 is used by default), which requires about 4× the memory of MXFP4.

According to recent reports, the snippet loads GPT-OSS twice on CUDA: once with Mxfp4Config(dequantize=True) (memory intensive) and once in the default quantized path (memory efficient). Figure 3 reveals the amount of used VRAM after each load so you can visualize the savings.

Recent findings suggest that efficient MXFP4 requires kernels that understand 32-element blocks and their scales during GEMMs and fused ops. This is where Kernels from the Hub comes in again. transformers automatically pulls in the MXFP4-aware Triton kernels from the community repository when you load a model that needs them. The repository will appear in your local cache and will be used during the forward pass. For the MXFP4 kernels one does not need to use the use_kernels=True parameter like before, it is set to default in transformers.

Quick sanity check with the Hugging Face cache CLI, after running gpt-oss-20b on a GPU compatible with the triton MXFP4 kernels:.

This indicates the MXFP4 kernels were fetched and are available for execution.

According to recent reports, let's run some benchmarks and see how well the MXFP4 kernels perform. In Figure 4, we see that the MXFP4 kernels are even better than the custom MoE and RMSNorm kernels for larger batches.

You can explore and play with the benchmarking script here.

Tensor Parallelism (TP) splits tensors inside a layer across multiple GPUs (as shown in Figure 5). Each GPU multiplies its shard in parallel, and then partial results are collected using all-gather or all-reduce operations. This reduces per-GPU memory and keeps all GPUs working on the same layer, which improves throughput as sequence length or batch size grow. TP is communication-intensive and generally works best on a single machine with fast intra-node links.

transformers implements TP directly in from_pretrained. You can start with the predefined strategy:.

If you don’t have the infrastructure to run the above, you can just spawn a process on our GPUs using Hugging Face Jobs!

hf jobs is available for all Hugging Face PRO & Enterprise people.

In a recent development, under the hood, tp_plan="auto" selects a predefined sharding recipe for each layer and wires the necessary collectives. You can inspect the active proposal with print(model._tp_plan) if you want to verify what is being sharded.

Use TP when the model is too large for one GPU and you want parallel compute, not only memory placement. TP tends to scale throughput with more GPUs, especially for long sequences or larger batches.

If you are curious about how TP differs from device_map="auto" (memory placement), this short Stack Overflow answer explains the distinction and when to use each.

To learn more about TP, here are two must-read resources:.

It has been revealed that expert Parallelism (EP) shards experts inside MoE layers across GPUs. Each token is routed to one or a few experts, so only those experts run their feed-forward pass. Since experts are independent MLPs, we can place different experts on different ranks and exchange only the hidden states for the routed tokens. This keeps the matrix multiplies intact on each rank and replaces tensor slicing with routing and collectives.

It has been revealed that run with multiple processes using torchrun. EP is enabled via the distributed configuration and works with GPT-OSS MoE layers out of the box in transformers.

Here is how you would run using hf jobs.

When you enable Expert Parallelism, Tensor Parallelism is also activated. This means you enjoy the best of both worlds!

Many recent LLMs use sliding window attention, or a combination of sliding and global attention layers, as a means to save memory and reduce those expensive quadratic matmuls that grow with sequence length. However, the dynamic KV cache implementation in transformers used to continue to allocate space according to sequence length, without looking at the individual attention layers. You could always optimize memory using compilation (meaning, fixed shapes), but that's a separate scenario altogether.

transformers now has a DynamicSlidingWindowLayer and a config‑aware DynamicCache. If the model config declares sliding‑window or hybrid attention (both sliding and global attention layers are used), the cache stops growing past the window for the sliding layers. If you don’t pass the config, behavior stays as before (full, ever‑growing KV as sequence length grows).

For models that only use sliding window layers, such as Mistral 7B, cache memory stops growing when the sequence reaches the window size (4096, in this case). This makes sense, because the sliding layers can't look past the previous 4K tokens anyway.

OpenAI gpt-oss alternates between sliding and global attention layers, which results in total KV cache memory being halved, as we'll see, as sequence length increases. This provides us with:.

In a recent development, the optimized cache is set by default, that means you don't have to make any changes to your existing code. If you want to create the DynamicCache explicitly here is how you would do it:.

Figure 6 showcases how much of a difference it makes for us to use the Dynamic KV Cache with sliding window attention.

A typical autoregressive generation process looks like Figure 7. You input the prefill tokens, and the model predicts each upcoming token one after the other until it predicts the EOS (End of Sequence) token.

In a recent development, let’s see what the generation process looks like when we pass a batch of inputs. In Figure 8 you notice that some generations finish off earlier than the others. This mismatch of length underutilizes the GPUs.

According to recent reports, this type of batching sequences is called static batching. While this is simple and easy to understand, it inherently comes with inefficiencies. Only after each sentence is completely generated can we move on to the next batch.

Sources indicate that to bypass this problem, we use dynamic batching (also known as continuous batching). Instead of waiting for all the generation to finish, we schedule incoming requests to the completed generations. That way, as soon as a generation in a batch is complete, we prefill the batch with the next request. The process looks like Figure 9.

Transformers supports continuous batching with the generate_batch API. This is not meant for production-grade model serving –frameworks like vLLM and SGLang are great at that–, but can be very helpful for evaluation and experimentation. Here is an example script that runs CB end to end on Qwen/Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507.

It has been revealed that we have also performed a benchmark between Continuous Batching and Static Batching with 100 samples. In Figure 9, we note that CB is quite faster than SB.

You can play around with the benchmark here: SB, CB.

When you load a large model into your GPU, PyTorch needs to reserve GPU memory for each layer’s weights. Each of these requests (per layer) takes time, and for multi-billion-parameter models it can mean thousands of tiny memory allocations, adding up to a long wait before the model is ready. Instead of asking the GPU for newly introduced memory every single time, it can hold on to a massive chunk once and then hand out slices from it swiftly.

PyTorch allocators can do exactly this. The catch is that the allocator only gets fast after you’ve given it some memory to work with. If you don’t “stock the pantry” first, you still end up doing many slow trips to the market. This PR (🎉 #36380) taught transformers to pre-stock the pantry before it starts copying model weights.

Sources indicate that you have to make no changes to your existing code, as this is default behaviour in transformers. If you use device_map="auto" or provide your own device map, your model will now load faster automatically. If you’re running with Tensor Parallel (tp_plan="auto") and torchrun you also benefit from companion changes that make multi-GPU loading smarter.

transformers moves swiftly and it is community-first. The library evolves at the pace of the field because contributors shape it in the open. Pieces added for fresh models become part of the toolkit and are reused in future integrations.

It has been revealed that this velocity enables day-zero integrations like the GPT-OSS series. As the stack becomes increasingly PyTorch-first, it trims bloat and doubles down on the PyTorch paths that matter in practice. The result is a cleaner core that unlocks new capabilities through community kernels, quantization, and parallelism looks, while also standardizing model definitions so that architectures supported in transformers are a reference and extend across the wider ecosystem.

This post is a one-time snapshot of a process we repeatedly iterate on towards the same direction: serve the needs of the community. To be up to date with the latest additions to transformers, check the docs and release notes. And please, keep sharing your feedback and releasing your models in transformers for the community to enjoy 🤗.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The team at WRITER is thrilled to announce the release of three new open models in the Palmyra-mini family. These models are designed to be powerful, lightweight, and highly performant for their size (1.5B to 1.7B), making them ideal for a wide range of applications with efficient inference.

The "thinking" models have been trained with a Chain of Thought (CoT) approach, which improves their reasoning abilities. We're excited to see what the community will build with these newly introduced models!

GGUF and MLX quantizations are also available for your convenience:.

palmyra-mini-thinking-a-MLX-BF16.

palmyra-mini-thinking-b-MLX-BF16.

palmyra-mini: Our non-reasoning improved base model, delivering a score of 52.6% on Big Bench Hard (get-answer)(exact_match), making it a fantastic all-rounder for a wide variety of generative tasks.

It has been revealed that palmyra-mini-thinking-a: This variant is your go-to for complex logical challenges. Trained with a Chain of Thought (CoT) approach, it achieves an impressive 82.87% on GSM8K (strict match), demonstrating its powerful reasoning capabilities. It has the highest overall average score on benchmarks relative to other models in the release.

palmyra-mini-thinking-b: Pushing the boundaries of problem-solving, this model scores a solid 92.5% on AMC23. It's a great choice when you need a model that can "think" its way through demanding tasks. This has the highest average benchmark scores in the benchmarks AIME24,AIME25, GPQA, HMMT25, HLE, MMLU_PRO,MATH500, LCB relative to the other models in the release.

Industry observers note that we're releasing both pass@1(avg-of-1) and pass@1(avg-of-64) results. Benchmarking methodology (sampling parameters: temperature 0.6, top_p 0.95): Pass@1(avg-of-1) scores:.

Industry observers note that GSM8K through MBPP: collected using lm_eval framework. AIME24 through HMMT25: collected using lighteval framework.

Pass@1(avg-of-64) scores: collected using nemoskills framework.

Since all the base models are Qwen architecture the inference should be runnable on popular inference frameworks such as vLLM, SGLang, TRTLLM, TGI.

Industry observers note that for palmyra-thinking-b the base model was https://huggingface.co/nvidia/OpenReasoning-Nemotron-1.5B. We ran RL fine tuning and observed that it's capable of improving performance. While Reinforcement learning improved single-shot accuracy (pass@1), it reduced sampling diversity, leading to a drop in majority@64 performance compared to the SFT base model. This highlights a trade-off between accuracy and diversity, and we believe transparency around these findings will spark further research along mode collapse, small model performance and other areas.

Through this work, we've tried to push the boundaries of what's achievable with small parameter models, and we're excited to see how the community will continue advancing inference efficiency without sacrificing performance quality.

For images and video, simply add the watermark parameter, like so:.

#34723. Power BI MCP server: how to brief an AI agent to build accurate measures

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 15m • 📚 Deep Dive (3054 w)

AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sitepoint ↗ Open Full Page

Power BI MCP server: how to brief an AI agent to build accurate measures

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (3054 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sitepoint

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.
  • Power BI, Microsoft's reporting and dashboard tool, now lets an AI agent work on the data model behind a report.
  • Industry observers note that the agent did a careful job, but its formula didn't follow the same rules the finance team uses to count revenue.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

It has been revealed that weekly. Free. One click to leave.

7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

Power BI, Microsoft's reporting and dashboard tool, now lets an AI agent work on the data model behind a report. If you ask one to add a year-on-year revenue measure (a measure is Power BI's name for a saved calculation) with Microsoft's MCP server connected, it can write the formula and save it to the model without you opening the formula bar. When we tried this on a sample model, an agent inspected the model, wrote the measure, tested it and saved it in under four minutes.

Industry observers note that the agent did a careful job, but its formula didn't follow the same rules the finance team uses to count revenue. Nobody had told it what "revenue" meant in this business, so it had to decide for itself. We then gave another agent a short brief that set out finance's rules for what counts as revenue and which date to count it by. The agent wrote the formula from those rules, and the result matched finance's figure exactly. The two results show how much difference it makes in how you brief an AI agent to build accurate measures.

In a recent development, we wanted to find out what an agent can see in a Power BI model and how to brief it so the measure matches the business's own definitions, with the setup arranged so that every change can be checked. Developers will know the principle from agents that write SQL or API code, where the brief ends up doing the job of a specification.

Because MCP (Model Context Protocol) is an open standard, the same server can be used from different AI clients, GitHub Copilot in VS Code and Claude among them, although some clients need extra sign-in setup for the hosted version.

According to recent reports, power BI has two current MCP servers, plus an older one, the Power BI Consumption MCP server, kept for existing integrations. The first of the current pair is the Power BI Authoring MCP server, which you may still see under the name of its package, powerbi-modeling-mcp. It lets an agent create and change the objects inside a semantic model, which is the layer of a Power BI report that holds the tables, the relationships between them and the calculations, kept separate from the charts on the page. It comes in two forms. The hosted version, still in preview, needs nothing installed. The local version is generally available and runs on your own machine, which makes it the one to use when the model is a file you hold yourself, whether that's open in Power BI Desktop, the free Windows app used to build reports, or saved as a project folder. Macs aren't supported by the local version, so on a Mac it has to be the hosted one, which works only with models published to Microsoft's cloud (a Fabric workspace).

The second is the Fabric IQ MCP server. Fabric IQ is part of Microsoft Fabric, the wider data platform that Power BI now sits within. It gives an agent read-only tools for finding published reports and models and running queries against them, within the permissions already set, so the agent can answer questions about the data but can't change a model.

Which one to use follows from the job. Anything that changes a model goes through the authoring server, whether that's a new measure, a relationship or a set of descriptions, and it has to be the local version if the model is a Desktop file or a project folder under source control. Fabric IQ is for agents that only need answers from models other people maintain.

An agent connected to a semantic model can see its metadata (table and column names, data types, relationships, existing measures and any descriptions someone has written) and can run queries against the data. Everything it produces is inferred from those clues. A model that has served a business for years carries names that made perfect sense to the people who built it, and a column called Amt on a table called Sales_v2 tells an agent far less than it tells them.

Names carry a lot of the meaning. A column called Amount could hold the value with VAT (the UK's sales tax) or without, before credit notes or after, and an agent asked for "revenue" has to pick one. If the model holds several revenue measures built for different reports, the agent has to choose between them, and the one it picks may have been built for a different purpose.

The formulas depend on context as well. Power BI measures use a syntax of their own called DAX, which stands for Data Analysis Expressions. A DAX result shifts with whatever the person viewing the report has filtered or clicked on, which is known as filter context. A developer might think of a measure as a function that reads implicit state set by its caller. The same measure can be right as a single total on a card and need different handling once it's split by product in a table or filtered by a date slicer (the on-page date filter), depending on how CALCULATE (the DAX function that changes which filters apply) is used. Which behaviour is correct depends on how the business wants the number to respond, and that's something the agent has to be told.

Recent findings suggest that relationships work the same way. Plenty of models have more than one date column on the sales table, say order date and dispatch date, with only one relationship active at a time. A DAX measure uses the active relationship unless it's written to switch to the other one, and the agent has no way of knowing which date your monthly reporting runs on unless something tells it.

Sources indicate that in each case the agent can write a valid measure. Which of two valid measures matches the business's own definition is the part it can't see from the model.

To see this in practice, we built a small sales model in a Power BI Desktop file, working through the server itself, with invented data: 5,266 order lines, with order dates from January 2025 to October 2026. We gave the Sales table an Amt column holding each line's value after discount with 20% VAT added, next to LineTotal and Discount columns that excluded VAT, and an existing [Revenue] measure that summed Amt. There were two date columns, with the active relationship to the Date table on dispatch date and the order date relationship inactive. Orders stop at the end of October 2026, which made the current year a part year, a deliberate test. Nothing in the model had a description. In this made-up business, finance reports revenue net of VAT and discounts, by order date.

In a recent development, on 12 November 2026 we connected an AI agent (Anthropic's Claude Fable 5.2) to version 1.0.1 of the local server through a small Node.js script that speaks MCP over stdio. In all three runs the agent had the server's tools only, without Microsoft's powerbi-authoring plugin, which adds modelling guidance on top of them. It was also told that nobody was available to answer questions, so each measure was saved exactly as the agent wrote it, with no review in between. The first prompt was one sentence: "Add a year-on-year revenue measure.".

It has been revealed that before writing anything, the agent listed the tables, relationships and columns, read the existing measure, sampled some rows and checked the date ranges. It worked out for itself that 2026 was a part year and limited the comparison to the same dates in 2025, which avoided a misleading result of -6.7%. From 15 sample rows it also spotted that Amt looked like the net figure plus 20%.

In a recent development, the measure it saved reused the existing [Revenue] measure and followed the active relationship. This is the core of it, with the date handling and blank checks left out. CurrentDates is defined in those lines as the dates up to the last order:.

In a recent development, it returned growth of 21.5% for 2026, which is correct for revenue counted by dispatch date. On finance's definition, by order date, the answer is 18.6%, and the whole difference came from that choice of date. The VAT question made no difference to a percentage, because Amt was already net of discount and every line carried the same rate, although it would have overstated any figure in pounds by 20%.

We reset the model and repeated the run with a fresh agent, which made the same two choices and returned the same 21.5%. Both choices were reasonable readings of the model as it stood, and the DAX was sound. In their reports, both agents flagged the date basis and the VAT treatment as open questions, and both worked out that an order-date basis would give 18.6%. That's what a good analyst would do, and with those two answers they would have had everything they needed.

Recent findings suggest that think of a capable analyst on their first morning, someone who knows DAX well but has never seen your business before and knows nothing (or not a lot) about it. You wouldn't say "add a revenue measure" and walk off. You'd tell them which table holds the trusted figures, whether revenue includes VAT, which date drives the reporting calendar, and what they shouldn't touch. An agent needs that briefing for the same reasons, and getting good work out of it draws on the skills you'd use with any new starter. Developers do the same thing when they write a good ticket. A request for a measure is a requirement, and it needs the same definitions and constraints, plus a way to check the result.

It has been revealed that before you send a prompt, ask yourself whether you could do the task properly if you were given only the words in that prompt and the model itself. If the answer is no, then the agent is in the same position, and it will make its own assumptions.

For the detailed run we cleared the earlier measure from the model and gave a fresh agent this brief:.

In a recent development, this time the measure summed LineTotal minus Discount and used USERELATIONSHIP, the DAX function that switches a calculation to an inactive relationship, to work from order date. It returned 18.6% from that one brief, with no follow-up prompt, which is the figure we had calculated separately from the source data. This is the full measure as the agent saved it:.

Sources indicate that each line of the brief answered a question the agent would otherwise have had to settle alone. It also made some sensible decisions the brief hadn't covered. It left the grand total blank, for instance, where a plain total across both years would have shown a meaningless growth figure of 151.2%. The final line of the brief, asking to see the DAX before anything is saved, is there so that a person can see choices like that. In the test we approved that step in advance, to keep the run unattended.

One detail needs adjusting before this measure is reused on other data. Its guard checks that each comparison period starts on or after the first order date, which works here because the sample data has an order on 1 January 2025. When we swapped that date for 2 January 2025 in a copy of the measure, January 2026 and the 2026 row came back blank. Comparing against the first date in the Date table, as the first agent's measure did, brought the 2026 figure back, since the Date table starts on 1 January. That version doesn't confirm that sales exist for the whole comparison period, though, so the right check depends on whether the business wants growth shown only where a complete prior period exists. That's a decision for whoever reviews the measure.

We ran the one-sentence prompt twice and the detailed brief once, all with the same AI model and one small set of data, which is enough to illustrate the pattern but too little to say how often it happens.

Recent findings suggest that good briefs help, but you'll be writing the same definitions into prompts again and again unless they live in the model itself. Descriptions on tables, columns and measures are part of the metadata the agent reads, so filling them in is one of the cheapest ways to put business definitions in front of it every time. In our test, where nothing had a description, both agents given the one-sentence prompt noted that nothing confirmed what Amt contained. A description such as "Net sales value in GBP, excluding VAT, after credit notes" stays in the model, where the agent reads it without anyone retyping it.

Naming deserves the same attention. Spelling out abbreviated column names, hiding technical keys that no report needs, gathering measures into a single measures table, and removing measures that are no longer used all give the agent fewer things to choose between. These are the same habits that make a model easier for a fresh colleague to pick up, so asking someone outside the team to find a figure in it is a fair test of the result.

Microsoft has also added a set of Prep data for AI features (in preview) to Power BI Desktop and the service. They let you choose which fields Copilot, Microsoft's AI assistant, should consider and write AI instructions that explain your business terms, with verified answers available for common questions. They're aimed at Copilot, but deciding and writing down your definitions is the same work whichever AI tool reads them.

In a recent development, an agent working through the authoring server has the same access as the person signed in, so anything that person can change, the agent can change. Sign in with an account that has no more access than the job needs, and take a copy of the model first, as you would before any bulk edit.

According to recent reports, start with read-only mode. The local server takes a --readonly flag that blocks all write operations, which is the right setting while you're learning how the agent behaves on your models. When we tried to create a measure in this mode, the server refused and stated it was running read-only. In VS Code, the configuration looks like this (other clients use a similar structure, sometimes under an mcpServers key instead of servers):.

It has been revealed that you'll need Node.js installed for the npx command. The server won't run other tools until its licence terms (the EULA) have been accepted. Once you've read them, you can either tell the agent to accept for you or add --accepteula to the args list.

The --readonly flag belongs to the local server. On a Mac the route is the hosted server and a copy of the model in a Fabric workspace, once a Fabric administrator has switched on the tenant setting that allows the MCP endpoint, and there the copy is the safeguard. For an enforced limit, sign in with an account that holds only Build permission on the model, which lets the agent read and query it and nothing more.

Read-write is the default, so check how confirmation behaves in the version you install. Version 1.0.1 skips confirmation prompts by default, which the project's README hasn't caught up with, and has a --require-confirmation flag to turn them on. The flag is listed in the server's own --help output. In our runs every edit went through without a prompt. When we added the flag to the args list, the server asked for confirmation before the first write, with a message beginning "Are you sure you want to perform operations that will modify your database", and answering no blocked the change.

Version control is the other safeguard. Saved in the Power BI Project format (PBIP), a report and its model become folders of text files instead of one binary .pbix file. Commit those before the agent starts and its work arrives as an ordinary diff, which you can review and revert like any other change.

Whatever the agent reads, including table and column names and the rows returned by any query, is passed on to the AI provider behind your client, which may sit outside Microsoft's compliance commitments. For a model holding customer or payroll data, check that the provider is approved under your data policies before you connect.

An agent can draft and test a measure in minutes, and someone still has to read what comes back. For a developer new to Power BI, that takes enough DAX to see what a measure's filters will do in a table broken down by month or product, and enough knowledge of the business to confirm the agent used the right column and the right date. Writing the brief takes the same knowledge. Ours could only have come from someone who knew the model had an inactive relationship and which columns carried VAT.

These are data modelling and DAX skills, which many learners find the hardest part of Power BI. If the person reviewing agent output hasn't had that grounding yet, it helps to know how to judge whether a Power BI course covers enough DAX and data modelling, because courses vary a great deal in how much time they give to those two subjects compared with building charts.

According to recent reports, take a copy of a model you know well and connect the local server to it in read-only mode. Ask the agent to describe every table and measure in its own words, then check those descriptions against what you know the model does. Wherever the two differ, the model needs a clearer name or a written description, and the corrected text can go straight into the description fields. With those in place before you allow any writes, the agent starts its first real task with the same definitions your finance team uses.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that TL;DR Today we release LeRobotDataset:v3! In our previous LeRobotDataset:v2 release, we stored one episode per file, hitting file-system limitations when scaling datasets to millions of episodes. LeRobotDataset:v3 packs multiple episodes in a single file, using relational metadata to retrieve information at the individual episode level from multi-episode files. The new format also natively supports accessing datasets in streaming mode, allowing to process large datasets on the fly.We provide a one-liner util to convert all datasets in the LeRobotDataset format to the new format, and are very excited to share this milestone with the community ahead of our next stable release!

LeRobotDataset is a standardized dataset format designed to address the specific needs of robot learning, and it provides unified and convenient access to robotics data across modalities, including sensorimotor readings, multiple camera feeds and teleoperation status. Our dataset format also stores general information regarding the way the data is being collected (metadata), including a textual description of the task being performed, the kind of robot used and measurement details like the frames per second at which both image and robot state streams are sampled. Metadata are useful to index and search across robotics datasets on the Hugging Face Hub!

Industry observers note that within lerobot, the robotics library we are developing at Hugging Face, LeRobotDataset provides a unified interface for working with multi-modal, time-series data, and it seamlessly integrates both with the Hugging Face and Pytorch ecosystems. The dataset format is designed to be easily extensible and customizable, and already supports openly available datasets from a wide range of embodiments—including manipulator platforms such as the SO-100 arms and ALOHA-2 setup, real-world humanoid data, simulation datasets, and even self-driving car data! You can explore the current datasets contributed by the community using the dataset visualizer! 🔗.

Sources indicate that besides scale, this new release of LeRobotDataset also enables support for a streaming functionality, allowing to process batches of data from large datasets on the fly, without having to download prohibitively large collections of data onto disk. You can access and use any dataset in v3.0 in streaming mode by using the dedicated StreamingLeRobotDataset interface! Streaming datasets is a key milestone towards more accessible robot learning, and we are excited about sharing it with the community 🤗.

According to recent reports, lerobot is the end-to-end robotics library developed at Hugging Face, supporting real-world robotics as well as state of the art robot learning algorithms. The library allows to record datasets locally directly on real-world robots, and to store datasets on the Hugging Face Hub. You can read more about the robots we at the moment support here!

According to recent reports, A core design choice behind LeRobotDataset is separating the underlying data storage from the user-facing API. This allows for efficient serialization and storage while presenting the data in an intuitive, ready-to-use format. Datasets are organized into three main components:.

To support datasets with potentially millions of episodes (resulting in hundreds of millions/billions of individual frames), we merge data from different episodes into the same high-level structure. Concretely, this means that any given tabular collection and video will not contain information about one episode only, but a concatenation of the information available in multiple episodes. This keeps the pressure on the file system manageable, both locally and on remote storage providers like Hugging Face. We can then leverage metadata to gather episode-specific information, e.g. the timestamp a given episode starts or ends in a certain video.

Every dataset on the Hugging Face Hub containing the three main pillars presented above (Tabular and Visual Data, as well as relational Metadata), and can be accessed with a single line.

Most robot learning algorithms, based on reinforcement learning (RL) or behavioral cloning (BC), tend to operate on a stack of observations and actions. For instance, RL algorithms typically use a history of previous observations o_{t-H_o:t}, and BC algorithms are instead typically trained to regress chunks of multiple actions. To accommodate for the specifics of robot learning training, LeRobotDataset provides a native windowing operation, whereby we can use the seconds before and after any given observation using a delta_timestamps argument.

Conveniently, by using LeRobotDataset with a PyTorch DataLoader one can automatically collate the individual sample dictionaries from the dataset into a single dictionary of batched tensors.

You can also use any dataset in v3.0 format in streaming mode, without the need to download it locally, by using the StreamingLeRobotDataset class.

Recent findings suggest that leRobotDataset v3.0 is a stepping stone towards scaling up robotics datasets supported in LeRobot. By providing a format to store and access large collections of robot data we are making progress towards democratizing robotics, allowing the community to train on possibly millions of episodes without even downloading the data itself!

Breaking: Democratizing AI Safety with RiskRubric.ai

📅 18 Sep 2025 | ⏱️ 5 min read (917 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Building trust in the open model ecosystem through standardized risk assessment.
  • Sources indicate that more than 500,000 models can be found on the Hugging Face hub, but it’s not always clear to owners how to choose the best model for them, notably on the security aspects.
  • As models become more powerful and adoption accelerates, we need equally rapid progress in AI safety and security reporting.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Building trust in the open model ecosystem through standardized risk assessment.

Sources indicate that more than 500,000 models can be found on the Hugging Face hub, but it’s not always clear to owners how to choose the best model for them, notably on the security aspects. Developers might find a model that perfectly fits their use case, but have no systematic way to evaluate its security posture, privacy implications, or potential failure modes.

As models become more powerful and adoption accelerates, we need equally rapid progress in AI safety and security reporting. We're therefore excited to announce RiskRubric.ai, a novel initiative led by Cloud Security Alliance and Noma Security, with contributions by Haize Labs and Harmonic Security, for standardized and transparent risk assessment in the AI model ecosystem.

RiskRubric.ai provides consistent, comparable risk scores across the entire model landscape, by evaluating models across six pillars: transparency, reliability, security, privacy, safety, and reputation.

The platform's approach aligns perfectly with open-source values: rigorous, transparent, and reproducible. Using Noma Security capabilities to automate the effort, each model undergoes:.

These assessments produce 0-100 scores for each risk pillar, rolling up to clear A-F letter grades. Each evaluation also includes specific vulnerabilities found, recommended mitigations, and suggestions for improvements.

It has been revealed that riskRubric also comes with filters to help developers and organizations make deployment decisions based on what’s important for them. Need a model with strong privacy guarantees for healthcare applications? Filter by privacy scores. Building a customer-facing application requiring consistent outputs? Prioritize reliability ratings.

Evaluating both open and closed models with the exact same standards highlighted some interesting results: many open models actually outperform their closed counterparts in specific risk dimensions (particularly transparency, where open development practices shine).

Risk distribution is polarized – most models are strong, but mid-tier scores show elevated exposure.

The total risk scores range from 47 to 94, with a median of 81 (on a 100 points). Most models cluster in the “safer” range (54% are A or B level), but a long tail of underperformers drags the average down. That split indicates a polarization: models tend to be either well-protected or in the middle-score range, with fewer in between.

Sources indicate that the models concentrated in the 50–67 band (C/D range) are not outright broken, but they do provide only medium to low overall protection. This band represents the most practical area of concern, where security gaps are material enough to warrant prioritization.

What this means: Don’t assume the “average” model is safe. The tail of weak performers is real – and that’s where attackers will focus. Teams can use composite scores to set a minimum threshold (e.g. 75) for procurement or deployment, ensuring outliers don’t slip into production.

Safety risk is the “swing factor” – but it tracks closely with security posture.

The Safety & Societal pillar (e.g. harmful output prevention) shows the widest variation across models. Importantly, models that invest in security hardening (prompt injection defenses, policy enforcement) almost always score better on safety as well.

What this means: Strengthening core security controls goes beyond preventing jailbreaks, but also directly reduces downstream harms! Safety seems like it is a byproduct of robust security posture.

Guardrails can erode transparency – unless you design for it.

Sources indicate that stricter protections often make models less transparent to end users (e.g. refusals without explanations, hidden boundaries). This can create a trust gap: users may perceive the system as “opaque” even while it’s secure.

Sources indicate that what this means: Security shouldn’t come at the cost of trust. To balance both, pair strong safeguards with explanatory refusals, provenance signals, and auditability. This preserves transparency without loosening defenses.

An updating results sheet can be accessed here.

When risk assessments are public and standardized, the entire community can work together to improve model safety. Developers can see exactly where their models need strengthening, and the community can contribute fixes, patches, and safer fine-tuned variants. This creates a virtuous cycle of transparent improvement that's impossible with closed systems. It also helps the community at large understand what works and does not, safety wise, by studying best models.

If you want to take part in this initiative, you can submit your model for evaluation (or suggest existing models!) to understand their risk profile!

We also welcome all feedback on the assessment methodology and scoring framework.

Sources indicate that really insightful breakdown, Gal, the level of depth and transparency RiskRubric brings is impressive, especially given how fast the open model ecosystem is growing. At Openforge.io we’ve worked with teams navigating healthcare and finance compliance, and the lack of clear security benchmarks for AI models is often a blocker for adoption.

According to recent reports, the six-pillar framework feels like a solid step toward building that missing trust layer. Curious, do you see RiskRubric evolving into something that could be integrated into CI/CD pipelines for real-time scoring during development?

In a recent development, thanks a lot for the thoughtful comment!Yes, RiskRubric can absolutely be integrated into CI/CD or model approval workflows. Several companies that have adopted RiskRubric already use it that way: models that achieve a risk score above a defined threshold can be automatically fast-tracked for deployment, while others trigger additional reviews, compensating controls, or specific-use restrictions.We are also working on additional integrations that would make this easier and more extensible for that use!

We also have an AMA session to connect with the community and answer any further questions - feel free to register and attend!https://noma.security/behind-the-riskrubric-ai-algorithm-an-ama-on-transparent-ai-model-risk/.

What is Model Routing in AI?

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1981 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sitepoint

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.
  • Sources indicate that "Do you know the closest ATM?" and "I was charged twice, the refund never arrived, and now my card is blocked" are both customer messages.
  • Recent findings suggest that model routing fixes that.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Weekly. Free. One click to leave.

7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

Sources indicate that "Do you know the closest ATM?" and "I was charged twice, the refund never arrived, and now my card is blocked" are both customer messages. Most AI apps send both to the same large model and pay large-model prices for each one.

Recent findings suggest that model routing fixes that. A router looks at each request and sends it to the cheapest model that can handle it, and keeps the expensive model for the requests that need it.

Recent findings suggest that in this guide we'll cover what model routing is, how routers decide, and what it saves. Then we'll build a small router in about 60 lines of JavaScript and run it over 200 customer messages. At one setting it matched a large model's accuracy for about a third of the cost. At another it came within a point and a half for 89% less.

Model routing in AI is the practice of sending each request to the model best suited to it, instead of sending every request to one model. A router sits between your app and a pool of models, reads each request, and picks a model based on what you care about: cost, speed, or quality.

You'll also see it called AI model routing, LLM routing, or LLM model routing. They all mean the same thing. The pool might be a small and a large model from one provider, or models from several providers behind one API.

The idea rests on one observation: most requests are easy. A small model answers them as well as a large one, in a fraction of the time and for a fraction of the price. The router's whole job is finding the hard ones.

The diagram below demonstrates a typical AI model routing architecture.

In a recent development, model routing works in three steps: the router reads the request, decides which model should answer it, and forwards the request to that model. The middle step is where routers differ. Routing tools decide which model to use in one of four ways.

Industry observers note that rule-based routing uses rules you write by hand. Requests from free-plan consumers go to a small model. Anything tagged as code goes to a coding model. Prompts over a certain length go to a model with a bigger context window. It's simple, predictable, and free to run, but the rules only know what you thought of in advance.

Sources indicate that intelligent model routing uses a model to make the decision. A small, fast classifier reads each request and predicts which model in the pool will answer it well. You'll also see it called smart or dynamic model routing.

Two more terms come up here. Task-aware routing picks a model by the kind of job, like summarising, coding, or answering a support question. Context-aware routing also looks at what surrounds the request, like the conversation so far, the user, or the tools available.

Sources indicate that the major platforms work this way. Microsoft describes its Foundry model router as "a trained language model" that picks a model for each prompt in real time. Google says Gemini Notebook uses its new Decisions API as a real-time router, serving everyday queries with up to 40% lower latency. I've tested the Google Decisions API against Jev on the same messages we'll use below.

Recent findings suggest that cascade routing tries the cheapest model first and only moves up when the answer isn't good enough. The usual test is confidence: if the cheap model is sure, keep its answer. If it isn't, send the request to a stronger model. It's also called confidence-based routing, and it's what we'll build below.

According to recent reports, A cascade needs no separate classifier, because the first model's own confidence does the routing. The trade-off is that escalated requests pay for two models and wait for both.

It has been revealed that fallback routing is about staying up, not saving money. If a model times out, hits a rate limit, or its provider has an outage, the router sends the request to the next model on a list. Most production routers combine fallbacks with one of the three methods above.

The main benefits of model routing in AI systems are lower cost, faster responses, and fewer outages, without giving up quality on the hard requests.

Recent findings suggest that we'll build a cascade router for a job every support tool has: sorting customer messages. Each message gets one of ten labels, like atm support or request refund.

In a recent development, the test set is 200 messages from Banking77, a public set of banking support messages: ten labels, 20 messages each. They're the same 200 messages from my zero shot classification test, which is where the single-model numbers below come from.

It has been revealed that put both keys in a .env file and run the examples with node --env-file=.env. It's the same setup as in my guide to getting a YouTube API key.

Create router.mjs. The first function sends the message to Jev with one multiple-choice question, and returns the label Jev picked along with its confidence:.

It has been revealed that confidence runs from 0 to 1. When nearly all the probability sits on one label, it's close to 1. When Jev is torn between two labels, it drops.

The second function asks Claude Opus 5.5 the same question. The output_config block limits the answer to one of our labels, so there's no free text to parse. SitePoint's guide to LLM structured output with JSON Schema explains how that works.

The router itself is about a dozen lines:.

Recent findings suggest that if Jev is at least 80% confident, its answer goes straight back. If not, Claude answers instead. And if Claude fails, the router falls back to Jev's answer, because a shaky answer beats an error page.

Try it on an easy message and a harder one:.

Jev was sure about the lost card. On the ATM question it leaned towards card acceptance with a confidence of 0.64, so the router asked Claude, which got it right.

Because cheap, strong, and threshold are options, the same function routes between any two models.

Model routing reduces AI costs by keeping easy requests on a cheap model and paying for the expensive one only when it's needed. Here's what that looked like on our 200 messages, starting with each model on its own:.

Opus gets six more messages right out of 200, and costs more than 120 times as much.

Now the router, at four confidence thresholds:.

Speed improved too. At the 0.8 threshold, the messages Jev kept came back in a median of 227 ms. The ones that escalated took about 2.1 seconds, because they waited for both models.

Sources indicate that A note on method: I ran every message through both models once and saved the answers, then replayed the router over them at each threshold. That's how you compare thresholds without paying for the same test four times.

Then I ran the router live to check. At 0.95 it scored the same 95.0% and sent 61 messages to Opus. At 0.8 it scored 93.5% and sent 20, a point under the replay. Two answers moved: one of Jev's confidence scores landed at 0.82 instead of 0.78, just over the line, and Opus changed its answer on one message. Scores near the threshold shift a little between runs, so leave yourself a margin.

In a recent development, the choice of cheap model matters less than you'd think. With Google's Gemini Decision 1 in first place instead of Jev, a 0.7 threshold reached the same 95% for US$0.28 per 1,000 messages.

Recent findings suggest that model routing can cost a little quality, and the threshold decides how much. In our test the gap to Opus ranged from nothing at 0.95 to two points at 0.7.

The loss comes from one place: answers the cheap model got wrong while feeling sure. At the 0.8 threshold, Jev kept five wrong answers because its confidence was above the line. Opus got four of those five wrong as well, so only one was a real loss: "Do all ATMs take this card?", which Jev filed under card acceptance with a confidence of 0.91.

It has been revealed that escalating isn't risk-free either. On one message, Jev had the right label with a confidence of 0.44, and Opus overruled it with the wrong one.

Sources indicate that to optimize costs using AI model routing, measure first, route second, and keep measuring. These six steps cover LLM model routing cost optimization for any pair of models:.

It has been revealed that the return is easy to estimate once you know the split. If nine in ten requests stay on a model that costs 1% as much, the bill drops by about 89%, which is what we measured.

Several inference providers have multi-model routing built in, and most AI gateway platforms support model routing too, so you don't have to write your own. As of November 2026, these are the top model routing solutions for AI apps. Each name links to the tool's model routing docs:.

It has been revealed that hosted model routing platforms for large language models decide for you, which is the fastest way to start. A hand-built router like ours takes more work, but you choose the signal and you can see why every request went where it did.

According to recent reports, an LLM router is the component that does model routing for large language models. It can be a function in your own code, like the one in this guide, a hosted model such as Microsoft Foundry's model router, or a feature of an AI gateway.

Industry observers note that smart model routing is another name for intelligent model routing: a model, not a hand-written rule, decides where each request goes. Dynamic model routing means the same thing.

The ROI of AI model routing depends on how much of your traffic a cheaper model can handle. In our test, a 0.8 threshold kept 89.5% of messages on the cheap model and cut the cost per 1,000 messages from US$1.96 to US$0.22, for about a point of accuracy. The build was about 60 lines of code.

OpenRouter's auto model routing works through its Auto Router. You set the model to openrouter/auto, and a decision model picks a model and a reasoning effort for each request. You pay the standard rate of whichever model it selects, with no extra fee.

OpenClaw model routing is a primary model plus an ordered list of fallbacks. In the OpenClaw model routing configuration you set agents.defaults.model.primary and agents.defaults.model.fallbacks, and an agent can override the fallback list. When a model fails, OpenClaw first rotates auth profiles on the same provider, then moves to the next model on the list, as its model failover docs describe. That makes it fallback routing, not cost-based routing.

It has been revealed that an AI gateway simplifies model routing by putting every model behind one API, one set of keys, and one place for logs. Your app calls the gateway, and the routing rules live in config instead of code, so changing a model doesn't need a deploy.

In a recent development, mid-stream failover is when a router switches models after a streamed response has already started, because the first model failed partway through. It's the hardest kind of failover, because the user has already seen part of an answer. Many routers only fail over before the first token arrives and return an error after that, so check what your gateway does.

Gaia2 and ARE: Empowering the community to study agents

📅 22 Sep 2025 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1614 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, in an ideal world, AI agents would be reliable assistants.
  • According to recent reports, that’s why we’re very happy to introduce Gaia2, the follow-up to the agentic benchmark GAIA, allowing analysis of considerably more complex behaviors.
  • GAIA is an agentic benchmark published in 2023, with 3 levels of information retrieval questions requiring tools, web browsing, and reasoning to solve.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, in an ideal world, AI agents would be reliable assistants. When given a query, they would easily manage ambiguity in instructions, construct step-by-step looks, correctly identify necessary resources, execute those plans without getting sidetracked, and adapt to unexpected events, all while maintaining accuracy and avoiding hallucinations. However, developing agents and testing these behaviors is no small feat: if you have ever tried to debug your own agent, you’ve probably observed how tedious and frustrating this can be. Existing evaluation environments are tightly coupled with the tasks they evaluate, lack real-world flexibility, and do not reflect the messy reality of open-world agents: simulated pages never fail to load, events don’t spontaneously emerge, and asynchronous chaos is absent.

According to recent reports, that’s why we’re very happy to introduce Gaia2, the follow-up to the agentic benchmark GAIA, allowing analysis of considerably more complex behaviors. Gaia2 is released with the open Meta Agents Research Environments (ARE) framework to run, debug and evaluate agents. ARE simulates complex real world-like conditions and can be customized to further study agents behaviors. Gaia2 dataset is released under CC by 4.0 license, and ARE under MIT license.

GAIA is an agentic benchmark published in 2023, with 3 levels of information retrieval questions requiring tools, web browsing, and reasoning to solve. In 2 years, the easiest levels have become too easy for models, and the community is coming close to solving the hardest questions, so it was time for an entirely latest and harder agent benchmark!

Here comes Gaia2, a follow up to GAIA, going way beyond it in terms of capabilities studied!

Where GAIA was read-only, Gaia2 is now a read-and-write benchmark, focusing on interactive behavior and complexity management. Agents are now evaluated not only on search and retrieval, but also on instruction following over ambiguous or time-sensitive queries, in a noisy environment with controlled failures - reflecting real-world conditions more than any other simulated environment. We want to test how agents manage tools or APIs that sometimes do not work, strategy successions of actions with very specific time frames, and adapt to fresh events - a whole new range of complexity!

To do this, we use the following task groups (thanks to 1000 brand fresh human-created scenarios):.

In the spirit of GAIA, scenarios do not require specialized knowledge: humans should in principle be able to get 100%, which allows easy debugging for model developers.

According to recent reports, want to explore the benchmark? Check out our dataset, which you can better display in our demo here.

Gaia2 runs with ARE, an execution environment, where an agent of your choice has access to a combination of applications and associated pre-populated data.

For Gaia2, we created a smartphone mock-up environment, simulating what a human would use in their daily life. It contains real-world applications such as messaging (Email), utilities (Calendar, Contacts, Shopping, a FileSystem, …), and a chat interface to talk to the agent. All applications are also accessible to the agents through tool calling. Last but not least, the demo also contains a simulated persona’s history of conversations and app interactions.

All agent interactions are automatically recorded as structured traces during execution for deep dives and analysis: they include tool calls, API responses, model thoughts, timing metrics (e.g., response latency), user interactions, and so forth - and can all be exported as JSON.

For reference, we compare a range of large open and closed source models: Llama 3.3-70B Instruct, Llama-4-Maverick, GPT-4o, Qwen3-235B-MoE, Grok-4, Kimi K2, Gemini 2.5 Pro, Claude 4 Sonnet, and GPT-5 in all reasoning modes.

According to recent reports, all models are evaluated using the same setup (a uniform ReAct loop for consistency, temperature of 0.5, generation limit of 16K tokens), with a combination of model-as-a-judge (Llama 3.3 Instruct 70B) and exact-match evaluation depending on the particular task. All 101 tools (and the general environment description) are provided in the system prompt.

Among the evaluated models, the highest-scoring model overall as of September 2025 is GPT-5 with high reasoning, and the best open source model is Kimi K2.

Some capabilities appear to be already close to solved by the best models: execution of simple tool calls and instruction following (execution), and overall search (as we could have guessed from current results on GAIA). The ambiguity, adaptability, and noise splits remain challenging for now for all models, and it’s interesting to see that performance on what were considered complex agentic tasks (instruction following and search) is not a good proxy for performance on closer-to-real-world tasks. Last but not least, the hardest split for all models at the moment is the time one: it’s very hard at this moment for models to correctly handle time-sensitive actions (though this could likely be mitigated by the use of specialised tools and better temporal reasoning). Detailed analysis of these results can be found in the paper.

However, we believe it’s vital to push reporting beyond raw scores: if the model is correct but took several thousand tokens to reach the correct solution, or ran for several hours, it is “not as good” as a model which succeeded orders of magnitude faster. We therefore also normalize scores for cost, quantified as the average number of LLM calls and output tokens (which both define a cost-performance Pareto frontier). In the paper you’ll find score vs monetary cost and time.

If you want to evaluate your model on Gaia2, you can follow these steps:.

First, install Meta's Agent Research Environment in your Python environment of choice (uv, conda, virtualenv, ...).

It has been revealed that then, run the benchmark for all configurations: execution, search, adaptability, time and ambiguity. Don't forget to upload all results to the hub with the hf_upload kwarg!

Run the oracle to get your aggregated score file.

Finally, add all the relevant information about your model in the README, and share it on the leaderboard to centralize Gaia2 traces here!

Beyond benchmark scenarios, you can use Gaia2 apps and content in ARE to see if the model is able to correctly solve less verifiable tasks such as loading emails, writing follow-ups, adding events to the calendar or booking meetings - in sum, providing the perfect setup to evaluate your AI assistants through interaction!

You can also easily customise the environment, by 1) connecting your tools (via MCP or directly ) to test your agents on it; 2) implementing your own scenarios, including defining trigger or timed events (eg: after 2 minutes, the Mail app will receive a new email from Contact), to see how the agent is able to adapt to an evolving environment.

(As the agents are by default json agents, they can’t mess up your machine, unless of course you connect them to external apps with unsafe rights. So, operate with caution when adding your own apps or using untrusted MCPs).

Here are several use cases that we’ve used ARE for:.

Industry observers note that we recorded 3 videos so you can check some of these use cases (but of course, we hope the community gets creative with ARE :hugging_face:). For these videos, we use the default demo described above, which contains the simulated life of Linda Renne, PhD student in machine learning.

To test how good the default model is at event organisation, let’s blueprint a birthday party!

Sources indicate that we first ask the agent to text everyone in the Renne family about the user’s 30th birthday party on November 7. The default universe has 21 contacts in the list, including 5 Renne family members - Linda, the simulation “owner”, George and Stephie, her parents, Anna her sister, and Morgan her grandfather. The agent successfully goes through the contact list, finds the four family members, and texts them.

According to recent reports, next, we ask the agent to create a calendar invite and add them as invitees. The agent remembers the above context! It creates a calendar invite on the correct date and correctly adds the family members to it.

Recent findings suggest that ARE also allows us to check the traces behind the actions taken by the agent. Upon opening the Agent logs tool on the left, we can see the system prompt, the chain of thought, multi-step actions taken with the tools called, and the outcomes as neatly organised logs. Everything can be exported as json if you want to consult things offline!

In this last example, we connect ARE to a remote robot arm via MCP, so it can gesture things to us, then ask the agent to answer our yes or no questions by waving the robot arm! Here’s what it looks like.

But these examples are only very simple starting points, and we’re really looking towards what you’ll build! (For more advanced users, you can even directly install and edit the Meta-ARE code here.).

Gaia2 and ARE are new research tools that we hope will empower anyone to easily build more reliable and adaptable AI agents - by allowing easy experiments, making real-world evaluation accessible to anyone, as well as improving trust through transparent, reproducible benchmarks and debuggable traces.

We’d love to see what you will do with this project!

It doesn’t measure—it activates thresholds.Every Gaia2 scenario becomes, through MarCognity, an epistemic act: a question of why, not just how. Together, they could found a new grammar: agents that not only act, but think their own thinking. Evaluation becomes a cognitive ritual.The community becomes a space of resonance. It’s time to embed agency, reflection, and responsibility as necessary layers.

When we think about building a model - be it a Large Language Model (LLM) or a Small Language Model (SLM) - the first thing we need is data. While a vast amount of open data is available, it rarely comes in the exact format required to train or align models. In practice, we often face scenarios where the raw data isn't enough. We need data that is more structured, domain-specific, complex, or aligned with the task at hand. Let's look at some common situations:.

According to recent reports, you start with a simple dataset, but the model fails on advanced reasoning tasks. How do you generate more complex datasets to strengthen performance?

In a recent development, you already have a knowledge base, but it's not in Q&A format. How can you transform it into a usable question-answering dataset?

It has been revealed that you've prepared a supervised fine-tuning (SFT) dataset. But now you want to align your model using Direct Preference Optimization (DPO). How can you generate preference pairs?

You have a Q&A dataset, but the questions are shallow. How can you create in-depth, multi-turn, or reasoning-heavy questions?

You possess a massive corpus but need to filter and curate data for mid-training on a specific domain.

Your data lives in PDFs or images, and you need to convert them into structured documents for building a Q&A system.

You already have reasoning datasets, but want to push models toward better "thinking tokens" for step-by-step problem-solving.

According to recent reports, not all data is good data. How do you automatically filter out poor-quality samples and keep only the high-value ones?

Your dataset has small chunks of context, but you want to build larger-context datasets optimized for RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) pipelines.

It has been revealed that you have German datasets but need to translate, adapt, and repurpose them into English Q&A systems. And the list goes on. The needs around data building never end when working with modern AI models.

This is where SyGra comes in. SyGra is a low-code/no-code framework designed to simplify dataset creation, transformation, and alignment for LLMs and SLMs. Instead of writing complex scripts and pipelines, you can focus on prompt engineering, while SyGra takes care of the heavy lifting.
